newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN: oil deal delayed until Iraq situation stable.
newsitem.headline: UN: oil deal delayed until Iraq situation stable.

text.p: A U.N. official said on Friday that the oil-for-food deal would be delayed until the situation in Iraq stablized and U.N. personnel would be safe.

Chinmaya Gharekhan, an undersecretary-general, told reporters: "It is safe to say that as long as the situation on the ground does not stabilise and security conditions do not permit us to deploy the necessary people on the ground, there would be...a delay."

But Gharekhan would not give any time frame on when he believed implementation of the accord, signed between Iraq and the United Nations on May 20, could go ahead. The deal allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food, medicine and other necessities for its people.

But he said the Dutch-based Saybolt firm, which has been hired to field about 14 oil inspectors in Iraq, had applied to the Baghdad government for visas and appeared ready to send some of its staff there shortly. Saybolt withdrew its advance team earlier this month when Iraqi forces entered the Kurdish inhabited north of the country.
However, Gharekhan said that Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali remained committed to early implementation of the plan and to "proceeding as fast as he can."

He was asked repeatedly whether the situation in northern Iraq would mean an alteration in the oil for food plan. Until recently Kurdish areas had not been under the control of the Baghdad government and the United Nations was to control all distribution of supplies there.
Gharekhan admitted that temporary detentions and departure of U.N. personnel, including local Kurds, did not make the situation easy during the fighting between two Kurdish factions.
"We don't know yet what has changed in the north and to what extent these things have changed," he said. "We will have to assess the situation there, whether things need to be modified in any way."
"We have to wait until the dust settles down and the situation on the ground becomes safe enough for us to start working on the ground," he said.

President Clinton has said that the plan was on hold because of the Iraqi action, and U.S. officials have suggested that Washington would make sure it was delayed. But other members of the U.N. Security Council are anxious that the plan go ahead as soon as possible.
